slides.say: p, q, r and s are different prime numbers. Given: x is equal to p cubed, times q squared, times s. And y is equal to p, times q to the power of five, times r, times s squared. What is the greatest common divisor of x and y?

So two numbers, already written in primes, and they ask for their greatest common divisor. It sounds like a big name, so let's say it in plain words. A common divisor divides both numbers, and the greatest one is the biggest number that divides both. And divisor means factor, so it's really the greatest common factor. [short pause] We'll solve it two ways, taking out a common factor, and then checking which choices divide both.
at: the biggest number that divides both

slides.say: [short pause] You already know how to take out a common factor. Picture x plus y, and ask what I can take out of both, in front of the brackets. Whatever comes out of both, divides both. And the biggest thing that comes out is the GCD.

So let's go prime by prime. p. x has p to the power of three, three p's, and y has just one p. How many p's are in both? Only one. So one p. Why not p cubed? Because y has only one p, so a number with two or three p's can't divide y.
at: x has p to the power of three

slides.say: q. x has q squared, two q's, and y has q to the power of five. Both of them have at least two q's, so q squared.
r. Is r in x? No, only y has it. So r can't divide x, and it stays out.
s. x has one s, and y has s squared, so one s. Each shared prime, at its lower power.
We found the shared factors p, q squared, and s. Multiply those shared factors to get the greatest common divisor: p times q squared times s. Choice number three is our answer.
at: Choice number three is our answer

slides.say: Now careful with choice number two. It takes every prime at its higher power, and that's too big, it doesn't even divide x. That's the smallest number that both of them divide, the least common multiple. It's the tool of the next question.

Let's see the lower power in numbers. Take a hundred seventy-two and a hundred twelve. What do they share? I have no idea yet, so I start by dividing by two. A hundred seventy-two is two times eighty-six, and eighty-six is two times forty-three. Forty-three is a prime. So a hundred seventy-two is two squared times forty-three.
at: A hundred seventy-two is two times

slides.say: A hundred twelve is two times fifty-six, fifty-six is two times twenty-eight, twenty-eight is two times fourteen, and fourteen is two times seven. So a hundred twelve is two to the power of four, times seven.
Not sure you broke it down right? Multiply back. Two to the power of four is sixteen, and sixteen times seven is a hundred twelve. Perfect.

So what do they share? Only twos. A hundred twelve has four of them, but a hundred seventy-two has only two. So the GCD is two squared, just four. A hundred seventy-two over four is forty-three, and a hundred twelve over four is twenty-eight. Such big numbers, and the biggest thing they share is four.
at: So the GCD is two squared

slides.say: [pause] Our second method, going through the choices. The GCD has to divide both x and y. So first, I throw out every choice that doesn't divide both, and then, from what's left, I take the biggest.
Choice number one has an r. x has no r at all, so it can't divide x. Out.
at: Choice number one has an r

slides.say: Choice number two has p cubed. y has only one p, so p cubed can't divide y. Out.
at: Choice number two has p cubed

slides.say: Choice number three, p, q squared, s. x has three p's, two q's and one s, enough of each. y has one p, five q's and two s's, enough again. So it divides both.

Choice number four, p, q, s, divides both too. But it's smaller, it has only one q, where choice number three has two. And they ask for the greatest. So choice number three. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
